title: Average 2. What does a typical case do?
hook: Each case infects 2 people on average. How many cases infect no one at all?

knows: R0 is the average number of people one case infects
an average can hide a spread of values
doesNotKnow: that spread between people is often very uneven
that with uneven spread most cases infect no one and a few cause most infections

misconception: Each case infects about R0 people.
objective: The learner can explain that with an average of 2 but very uneven spread (k = 0.1), about 74% of cases infect no one and a few cases cause most infections, so the average hides who drives an outbreak.

claims.text: Individual variation in spread can be modelled by a negative binomial offspring distribution with mean R and dispersion k; small k means very uneven spread.
claims.source: Lloyd-Smith J.O., Schreiber S.J., Kopp P.E. & Getz W.M. (2005) Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence, Nature 438:355-359.

claims.text: With mean 2 and k = 0.1, the share of cases that infect no one is (k/(k+R))^k = (0.1/2.1)^0.1 = 0.74; with even (Poisson) spread it is e^-2 = 0.14.
claims.source: Negative binomial P(0) = (k/(k+R))^k = 0.7375; Poisson P(0) = e^-2 = 0.1353. Recomputed in node (artifacts/scratch/w2life/check.mjs).

claims.text: On the stage's 100 cases: very uneven spread gives 74 who infect no one and the top 10 causing 165 of 200 infections; even spread gives 14 who infect no one, a total of 199 and no case above 7 in this picture; the in-between setting (k = 1) gives 33 and a total of 201. The counts are rounded.
claims.source: Each case gets the mean of its 1% slice of the distribution, rounded (expected shape, no random draw), replicated in artifacts/scratch/w2life/check2.mjs. Grid positions use an untuned seed (mulberry32(11)) and carry no information.

claims.text: When a few cases cause most spread, an average of 2 hides who drives an outbreak: the rare large spreaders can decide whether one takes off (most chains of transmission die out).
claims.source: Lloyd-Smith et al. (2005) Nature 438:355-359 (higher extinction probability of introductions for small k).

claims.text: The 'very uneven' setting (negative binomial with k = 0.1) is an illustration, not a measured value for any named disease; the 100 cases are an expected shape, not one random outbreak.
claims.source: Brief choice (company/domains/briefs/life.md #15); stated in the reveal and the stage says toy model.

recall.question: Two outbreaks both average 2 new infections per case. In outbreak A, spread is very uneven. Compared with B (even spread), A has…
options: more cases that infect no one, and a few that infect many
the same number of cases that infect no one
fewer cases that infect no one
recall.why: The same average can come from everyone infecting about 2, or from most infecting nobody and a few infecting dozens.
